tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README establishes this project's core purpose: a 3-tier bridge that lets MCP-capable AI clients (Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot, Codex, Gemini CLI) interact with a live Foundry VTT game world through natural language. The architecture flows stdio → TCP 31414 → WebSocket 31415 → browser, and everything that follows in this tour is an elaboration of that single chain. Start here to understand why each subsequent component exists and what role it plays.

tour.title: MCP Stdio Entry Point
tour.description: The stdio wrapper (`index.ts`) is the face that the AI client sees — it speaks the MCP protocol over stdin/stdout and forwards every tool call to the backend process over TCP port 31414. It implements a `BackendClient` with exponential-backoff retry and can auto-spawn the backend if it is not yet running, so the user never has to start processes in the right order manually. This file is intentionally thin: its only job is process management and protocol bridging, keeping the heavy orchestration in `backend.ts` which we will see next.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript class inheritance and interface implementation (`implements BackendClient`) allow this thin wrapper to swap out the transport layer independently of tool logic — a classic separation of concerns enforced by the type system.

tour.title: Backend Orchestrator & Tool Registry
tour.description: The backend (`backend.ts`) is the nerve centre of the MCP server: it acquires a PID-based file lock to prevent duplicate instances, registers all 50+ tool handlers with `ToolRegistry`, and starts the TCP control socket that receives dispatched calls from the stdio wrapper. `ToolRegistry` is deliberately simple — a name-keyed map of async handler functions — because the real complexity lives in the tool modules themselves. The fan-out ranking confirms this is the most structurally significant file on the server side, with 61 outbound import edges.
tour.languageLesson: The discriminated-switch dispatch pattern used here (matching on a string `toolName` to call a handler) is a common alternative to a class hierarchy when you want handlers to be individually tree-shakeable modules rather than methods on a god-object.

tour.title: Shared Contract: Types & Constants
tour.description: The `shared` package is the single source of truth that both the MCP server (Node.js) and the Foundry module (browser) import. `types.ts` defines the `MCPQuery` / `MCPResponse` wire format, actor shapes, and compendium structures, while `constants.ts` pins all socket event names and default port values. `shared/src/index.ts` is the barrel that re-exports everything with a fan-in of 82 — the highest in the entire codebase — confirming that nearly every other module ultimately depends on these definitions. Changing a type here has ripple effects across both packages.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript's barrel pattern (`export * from './types'`) in `shared/src/index.ts` creates a single import path for consumers. This is especially valuable in a monorepo where the same types must be consumed by packages targeting different runtimes (Node.js vs browser).

tour.title: Zod Schema Layer
tour.description: Every MCP tool input is validated by a Zod schema defined in `shared/src/schemas/`, aggregated by the barrel `shared/src/schemas/index.ts`. These schemas serve a dual purpose: they generate the JSON Schema objects that the MCP protocol requires in each tool's `inputSchema` declaration, and they act as a runtime guard on the Foundry module side before any Foundry API call is made. The `create-custom/index.ts` file is a particularly instructive example — it assembles a discriminated union across 26 WFRP4e item subtypes and dispatches to per-subtype payload builders, showing how Zod's `.discriminatedUnion()` replaces a large switch statement.
tour.languageLesson: Zod discriminated unions (`z.discriminatedUnion('action', [...])`) are ideal for action-based tool APIs because TypeScript narrows the payload type to the exact variant at the call site — you get both runtime validation and compile-time type narrowing from a single schema definition.

tour.title: WebSocket Bridge: Client & Connector
tour.description: The bridge between the MCP server and the Foundry browser is split across two files. `foundry-connector.ts` is the low-level WebSocket server on port 31415: it accepts the browser connection, maps each outbound query to a pending `Promise`, and resolves or rejects it when the matching response arrives. `foundry-client.ts` wraps that connector with a higher-level facade — `connect()`, `disconnect()`, `query()`, and connection-state introspection — that tool handlers call without knowing about WebSocket internals. This two-layer design makes unit testing possible: tools import `FoundryClient` and mock its `query()` method.
tour.languageLesson: The request-response correlation pattern used in `foundry-connector.ts` (storing a `Map<correlationId, {resolve, reject}>` of pending Promises) is the standard way to turn a duplex message stream into async/await function calls. Each query gets a UUID so the matching response can resolve the right Promise even if responses arrive out of order.

tour.title: Tool Handler Pattern: BaseTool & Character Tools
tour.description: All 50+ MCP tool modules extend the abstract `BaseTool` class, which provides the shared `protected query()` method that forwards calls through `foundry-client.ts`. This ensures every handler goes through the same error-scrubbing and response-unwrapping path. `character.ts` and `manage-character.ts` are the best entry points for understanding a complete tool: `character.ts` shows a read-only handler with rich response formatting (extracting stats, items, conditions, active effects), while `manage-character.ts` shows the discriminated-union action-routing pattern used by every write tool.
tour.languageLesson: The abstract class pattern here enforces a contract without dictating implementation: every subclass must declare `toolDefinition` (the JSON Schema the MCP client sees) and `handle()` (the logic), while `BaseTool` owns the transport concern. This is the Template Method design pattern applied to MCP tools.

tour.title: Foundry Module Entry Point
tour.description: On the browser side, `main.ts` is the Foundry VTT module's bootstrap: it registers module settings, installs runtime error capture, and wires three Foundry lifecycle hooks (`init`, `ready`, `socketlib.ready`) to start the `FoundryMCPBridge`. The bridge then starts `socket-bridge.ts` on port 31415, which is the client-side counterpart of the `foundry-connector.ts` we saw in Step 6. Notice that the module uses Foundry's hook system rather than a direct call chain — this is because Foundry's API is not available until the `ready` hook fires, so the module must defer initialization.
tour.languageLesson: Foundry VTT's hook system (`Hooks.once('ready', ...)`) is analogous to DOM `DOMContentLoaded`: it decouples module initialization from Foundry's own load sequence. The `socketlib.ready` hook specifically waits for the SocketLib dependency to register, demonstrating multi-dependency initialization ordering.

tour.title: Query Dispatch & Data Access
tour.description: The `QueryHandlers` class in `queries.ts` is the Foundry-side equivalent of `backend.ts` — a central routing table that maps incoming MCP command strings (e.g., `warhammer-mcp.getCharacter`) to the appropriate handler. With a fan-out of 54 it imports every document handler and delegates to them. `data-access.ts` sits beneath the handlers and wraps raw Foundry API calls (`game.actors.get()`, `actor.update()`, etc.) in a typed service class, keeping Foundry's global-variable API from leaking into test code.

tour.title: Transaction Safety & Permissions
tour.description: Every write operation in the Foundry module passes through two guards before touching Foundry data. `permissions.ts` checks that the calling user is a GM and that `allowWriteOperations` is enabled in module settings — a single gate that all 22 document handlers share. `transaction-manager.ts` wraps multi-step writes in an atomic unit with rollback support, so a failed mid-sequence update (e.g., updating career then failing to update skills) does not leave the actor in a partially-modified state. The `wrappedWrite` helper exported here is the most-imported file on the Foundry side (fan-in 20).
tour.languageLesson: The wrappedWrite pattern (permission check → execute → verify persisted value) implements the Post-condition Verification principle: rather than trusting that a write succeeded, the module re-reads the document and compares expected vs actual field values, catching Foundry hook vetoes and read-only field drift.

tour.title: CRUD Factory Utilities
tour.description: Rather than writing boilerplate create/read/update/delete logic for every Foundry document type, the module uses two factory functions. `embeddedCRUDFactory.ts` generates full handler sets for scene-embedded objects (lights, sounds, tiles, templates) with a GM gate and post-write verification included. `flatWorldCRUDFactory.ts` handles top-level world documents with standardized error tagging. Together these two factories eliminate hundreds of lines of duplicated code across the 22 document handlers, and both route through `transaction-manager.ts`'s `wrappedWrite` — so all the safety guarantees from Step 10 apply automatically.
tour.languageLesson: Higher-order factory functions that return handler objects (`createEmbeddedCRUDHandlers<T>({ ... })`) are TypeScript's answer to code generation. The generic type parameter `T` carries the document's data shape, so the returned handlers are fully typed without any casting at the call site.

tour.title: WFRP4e Item Creation System
tour.description: The WFRP4e item creation system is one of the deepest vertical slices in the codebase and illustrates the full pipeline end-to-end. `create-custom-item.ts` on the server side validates a discriminated union input via the schema from Step 5, then sends a single query over the WebSocket bridge from Steps 6-8. On the Foundry side the query handler constructs the WFRP4e-specific `system.*` payload using the `buildSystemForSubtype` dispatcher in `shared/src/schemas/create-custom/index.ts`. All 26 item subtypes (weapons, spells, careers, mutations, module-specific items like runes and chanties) share the `CreateCustomItemCommon` base schema from `shared/src/schemas/create-custom/common.ts`.
tour.languageLesson: The foreign-key catalog in `fk-catalog.ts` encodes ~20 cross-document reference relationships as data rather than code. This allows a single audit walker to check all FK integrity without knowing which specific fields link which document types — a data-driven approach that scales as new document types are added.

tour.title: MCP Client Configuration
tour.description: The `configs/clients/` directory contains ready-to-paste configuration files for every supported AI client: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code Copilot, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI. Each file is just a few lines that tell the client where to find the compiled `backend.js` and what environment variables to pass. The `claude_desktop_config.example.json` at the root is the simplest example; reading it alongside the architecture from Step 1 makes the stdio transport concrete — the AI client launches `node backend.js` as a child process and communicates over stdio.

tour.title: Release Pipeline
tour.description: The GitHub Actions workflow `build-complete-release.yml` shows how this multi-package monorepo is shipped: it builds an NSIS Windows installer (which bundles Node.js for end users who don't have it), packages the Foundry module as a zip that Foundry's package manager can install directly, creates a GitHub Release with all artifacts, and optionally pings the Foundry package registry. Understanding this pipeline explains the dual-artifact nature of the project — users install one artifact in Foundry VTT and the other as a system service on their machine.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions release pipelines triggered on `push: tags: ['v*']` let you version by git tag. The workflow uses `actions/upload-artifact` to share build outputs between parallel jobs and `softprops/action-gh-release` to assemble the final GitHub Release — a common monorepo release pattern.

tour.title: Developer Reference & Tests
tour.description: The developer guide `docs/INSTRUCTIONS.md` is the companion to the README — it covers the add-a-tool workflow step by step, WFRP4e-specific implementation details (XP tier cost tables, UUID construction, `skipDialog` gotchas), and a new-session startup checklist. The `tests/skills/_harness.ts` file is the foundation of the end-to-end skill tests: it provides `mockMcpCall`, `callMcp`, and `invokeSkill` utilities that let skill tests exercise complete WFRP4e scenarios (advancing a character, casting a spell, running combat) against mock Foundry responses, validating that the full bridge chain produces the correct sequence of tool calls.
